subtopic_detail: Cyclical pelvic pain with urinary retention in an adolescent with normal breast development and no menarche
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 14 year old girl brought in by her mother because she has not passed urine since yesterday morning and her lower tummy is sore and swollen.

She has never had a period. For the past six months she has had cramping lower abdominal pain lasting three or four days that comes back about every four weeks and has been getting worse each time. Her breasts began developing at eleven and she has had underarm and pubic hair for two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development, tender suprapubic mass palpable to the umbilicus and dull to percussion, inspection of the introitus shows a tense bulging bluish membrane, no abdominal guarding or rebound
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, bladder scan shows a residual volume of 780 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Pass an indwelling catheter and arrange outpatient gynaecology review
options.rationale: Catheterisation is a reasonable holding measure that relieves the retention while theatre is organised, but discharging her with a catheter leaves an obstructed upper genital tract that will continue to accumulate blood and progressively distend. The obstruction itself is what has to be relieved. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.text: Refer for surgical incision of the obstructing membrane in theatre
options.rationale: Normal breast and pubic hair development shows the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis is working and oestrogen is being produced, so the absence of menstruation with cyclical pain and a bulging bluish membrane is outflow obstruction rather than a failure to menstruate. Incision under anaesthesia drains the accumulated blood, relieves the retention and is definitive. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

options.text: Request a karyotype and measure the serum testosterone concentration
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement are how complete androgen insensitivity is identified in a phenotypic girl with primary amenorrhoea, and that condition is suggested by absent or sparse pubic and axillary hair with normal breast development. This girl has Tanner stage 4 pubic hair and a visibly distended obstructed tract. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Give a progestogen course and observe for a withdrawal bleed afterwards
options.rationale: A progestogen challenge tests whether an oestrogenised endometrium will shed and is used in secondary amenorrhoea when the outflow tract is known to be patent. Provoking endometrial shedding above a closed outflow tract would add to a collection that already has nowhere to drain. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive to suppress her cyclical symptoms
options.rationale: Menstrual suppression relieves cyclical pain in endometriosis and in dysmenorrhoea, where the outflow tract is open and the problem is the bleeding itself. Using it here would mask the monthly pain that is the only warning sign while the obstructed collection continues to enlarge and threaten the tubes. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is separated at the bedside by whether secondary sexual characteristics have developed, because normal breast development means oestrogen has been produced and shifts the problem to the outflow tract or the uterus. An imperforate hymen is the commonest obstructive cause, occurs in about one in two thousand girls, and presents at the age of expected menarche with months of escalating cyclical pain from blood accumulating in the vagina and uterus. A large collection compresses the bladder neck and urethra, so acute urinary retention in an adolescent who has never menstruated is close to diagnostic. Treatment is surgical incision and drainage under anaesthesia with a cruciate or elliptical incision, since simple needle aspiration risks ascending infection and reaccumulation. Delay allows retrograde spill through the tubes, which is associated with endometriosis and tubal damage.
key_points: Normal breast and pubic hair development localises the problem to the outflow tract
Escalating cyclical pain with no menarche is obstruction until proven otherwise
A distended vagina compresses the urethra and causes acute urinary retention
Incision and drainage under anaesthesia is definitive, not needle aspiration
Delayed drainage allows retrograde spill with tubal damage and endometriosis
explanation.pearls: Inspect the introitus before ordering any test in an adolescent with primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pain: a tense bluish bulging membrane makes the diagnosis in seconds, and imaging or hormone profiling merely delays a girl who is in retention from getting to theatre the same day.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology

subtopic_detail: Burning nipple pain between feeds with biphasic colour change of the nipple triggered by cold
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman who is five weeks postpartum with her first baby. She describes a deep burning pain in both nipples that starts as the baby comes off the breast and lasts about twenty minutes, and says the nipple turns white, then dusky, then bright red and throbbing before the pain eases.

It is worst when she feeds in the lounge room in the early morning and barely happens at all after a warm shower. She has used a topical antifungal cream for three weeks on advice from a pharmacist with no change. She has no fever, and the baby is gaining weight well and feeds for twenty minutes before releasing the breast himself.

data_table.Examination: Nipples intact with no fissures, no shiny or flaking areolar skin, no palpable breast lump and no wedge shaped erythema, baby's tongue and buccal mucosa clear with no white plaques, latch observed to be deep with a rounded nipple on release
data_table.Investigations: Nipple swab shows no growth of Candida species

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a two week course of oral fluconazole for deep breast candidiasis
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal treatment is used for ductal candidiasis, which typically follows antibiotic use and comes with shiny or flaking areolar skin or oral plaques in the infant. Three weeks of topical antifungal has already failed and the swab grew nothing, so continuing down this path treats a diagnosis twice excluded. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain)

options.text: Apply a topical corticosteroid ointment to both nipples after every feed
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid is the treatment for nipple eczema or contact dermatitis, which presents with itch, scaling and erythema of the areolar skin between feeds. The skin here is intact and the pain is episodic and colour linked rather than continuous and itchy. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nipple pain in breastfeeding)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nipple pain in breastfeeding

options.text: Refer the baby for division of a posterior tongue tie under local anaesthesia
options.rationale: Restricted tongue movement causes nipple pain by compressing the nipple against the hard palate, which leaves the nipple wedge shaped or blanched along one edge as it is released. This baby releases the breast spontaneously with a rounded nipple and is gaining weight, so transfer and attachment are not the problem. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain)

options.text: Advise applying dry warmth immediately after feeds and avoiding cold exposure
options.rationale: A biphasic or triphasic colour change of the nipple with burning pain that begins on detachment and is provoked by cold is arteriolar vasospasm, the nipple equivalent of Raynaud phenomenon, and it responds to keeping the nipple warm and dry as the baby comes off. Conservative measures, along with reducing caffeine and nicotine, resolve most cases, with oral nifedipine reserved for pain that persists despite them. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain)

options.text: Arrange expression and bottle feeding of breast milk until the pain resolves
options.rationale: Moving to expressed milk protects damaged nipples in severe trauma and preserves supply while a wound heals, but it does not stop vasospasm, which is triggered by the temperature change on detachment and occurs equally after pumping. It also introduces an unnecessary interruption to direct feeding. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nipple pain in breastfeeding)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nipple pain in breastfeeding

explanation.summary: Nipple vasospasm is frequently misdiagnosed as candidiasis because both cause burning pain that continues between feeds, and women commonly complete several courses of antifungal treatment before the right diagnosis is made. The discriminating features are the timing, beginning as the baby detaches rather than during the feed, the trigger, which is cold air on a wet nipple, and the visible colour sequence of blanching followed by cyanosis and then reactive hyperaemia. It is more common in women with a personal or family history of Raynaud phenomenon, migraine or autoimmune disease, and is aggravated by caffeine, nicotine and beta blockers. First line management is behavioural, covering the nipple with a warm dry breast pad as the baby comes off, warming the room, avoiding wet compresses and reducing vasoconstrictors. Nifedipine is effective for refractory cases and is compatible with breastfeeding.
key_points: Pain starting on detachment and provoked by cold separates vasospasm from candidiasis
White then dusky then red colour change of the nipple is the diagnostic sequence
Failure of an adequate antifungal trial argues strongly against candidiasis
Dry warmth on detachment plus reducing caffeine and nicotine is first line
Nifedipine is the pharmacological option and is compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Tell her to avoid the intuitive response of applying a warm wet washer after feeds: evaporative cooling from the damp cloth is itself a potent trigger, and dry warmth from a heat pack over a dry breast pad is what aborts the vasospasm.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nipple pain in breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: Pain over the pubic symphysis and posterior pelvis in the third trimester with a positive provocation test
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. She reports pain at the front of her pelvis that grinds when she rolls over in bed, climbs stairs or stands on one leg to dress, and says she waddles by the end of the day.

The pain is also felt across the back of her pelvis just below the dimples at the base of her spine. She has had no vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid, no tightenings, and the baby is moving normally. She had similar but milder symptoms in her first pregnancy which settled after the birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 145 per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness over the pubic symphysis and both sacroiliac joints, posterior pelvic pain provocation test positive bilaterally, straight leg raise negative, no renal angle tenderness, power and reflexes in both legs within normal limits, symphysiofundal height 28 cm
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for protein, nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a pelvic support belt and an exercise programme
options.rationale: Pelvic girdle pain is a mechanical problem of load transfer through the pelvic ring, and the treatment with the best evidence is an individualised programme of stabilising exercise combined with a support belt worn low over the greater trochanters. Physiotherapy also covers activity modification such as keeping the knees together when turning and avoiding single leg loading. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

options.text: Advise strict bed rest until the symptoms settle and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Rest relieves the pain transiently because it removes load from the pelvic ring, but prolonged immobility deconditions the stabilising musculature and increases venous thromboembolic risk in pregnancy. Graded activity rather than avoidance is what improves function. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe a regular oral opioid analgesic for the remainder of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Opioids are reserved for short term use in severe pain that has not responded to physical treatment and simple analgesia, and regular third trimester use risks neonatal withdrawal and respiratory depression at birth. They also do nothing for the load transfer problem that is generating the pain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Analgesics in pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Analgesics in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when there are neurological signs, fever, a history of malignancy or trauma, none of which is present with a negative straight leg raise and normal power and reflexes. Pelvic girdle pain is diagnosed by provocation testing rather than by imaging findings, which correlate poorly with symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

options.text: Plan a caesarean section at 39 weeks to protect the pelvis during labour
options.rationale: Caesarean birth is not protective against pelvic girdle pain and is associated with slower postnatal recovery of function, so it is not offered on the basis of the pain alone. The relevant intrapartum planning is to document a comfortable range of hip abduction and to avoid exceeding it in lithotomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pelvic girdle pain affects around one in five pregnancies and arises from altered load transfer through the sacroiliac joints and pubic symphysis under the influence of relaxin and a changing centre of gravity. The diagnosis is clinical and rests on provocation tests, most usefully the posterior pelvic pain provocation test and palpation of the symphysis, together with the characteristic pattern of pain on turning in bed, stair climbing and single leg loading. It is separated from lumbar radiculopathy by a negative straight leg raise with normal power and reflexes, and from urinary infection or preterm labour by the absence of urinary symptoms, bleeding and tightenings. Management is physiotherapy led, with a pelvic support belt, stabilising exercise, activity modification and paracetamol, and around nine in ten women recover within a few months of birth. Persistent severe symptoms warrant postnatal reassessment, since untreated pain is a risk factor for postnatal depression.
key_points: Pain on turning in bed, stairs and single leg loading is the characteristic pattern
Diagnosis is by provocation testing, not by imaging
A negative straight leg raise with normal reflexes excludes radiculopathy
A support belt worn low over the greater trochanters plus exercise is first line
Around ninety per cent of women recover within months of birth
explanation.pearls: Check where she is wearing the belt: a pelvic support belt worn around the waist does nothing, whereas the same belt sitting low over the greater trochanters below the anterior superior iliac spines compresses the pelvic ring and often relieves symphyseal pain within days.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook: Analgesics in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal hand numbness in the third trimester in a radial distribution with preserved power and bulk
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a woman at 32 weeks in the antenatal clinic who says both her hands go numb and buzzing at night and wake her, and that she shakes them over the side of the bed until the feeling comes back.

The numbness affects her thumb, index and middle fingers and spares her little finger. She drops her coffee cup occasionally in the mornings but can do up buttons and open jars normally. She has no neck pain and no pain radiating down her arms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 per minute
data_table.Examination: Sensory blunting over the palmar surface of the thumb, index and middle fingers bilaterally, Phalen test reproduces symptoms within 40 seconds, Tinel sign positive at the wrist, abductor pollicis brevis power and bulk within normal limits, reflexes symmetrical, no oedema beyond mild ankle swelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid stimulating hormone and fasting glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before deciding on any treatment
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies confirm the site and severity of compression and are needed when the diagnosis is uncertain or when surgery is being planned. With a textbook history, a positive Phalen and Tinel sign and no motor deficit, they would not change the first line treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Inject corticosteroid into the carpal tunnel at the wrist crease bilaterally
options.rationale: Corticosteroid injection gives effective short term relief and is a legitimate second line option in pregnancy when splinting has failed, but it carries a small risk of nerve injury and of transient hyperglycaemia. It is not the starting point for symptoms that will resolve after delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Refer to a hand surgeon for consideration of carpal tunnel decompression
options.rationale: Surgical decompression is indicated for persistent symptoms with thenar wasting or motor weakness, which signal axonal loss that will not recover with time. Normal abductor pollicis brevis power and bulk means there is no such indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe a reducing course of oral prednisolone over the next fortnight
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid produces modest short lived improvement in carpal tunnel syndrome outside pregnancy, but it raises maternal glucose and blood pressure at a gestation when both are already under surveillance. The risk to benefit balance does not support it for a self limiting condition. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Corticosteroids)

options.text: Supply wrist splints holding the wrist in neutral to be worn overnight
options.rationale: Symptoms occur at night because the wrist flexes during sleep and raises carpal tunnel pressure, so a splint that holds the wrist neutral abolishes the provoking posture and is the first line treatment. Pregnancy related carpal tunnel syndrome is driven by fluid retention and resolves in the great majority of women within weeks to months of delivery, which makes conservative treatment the appropriate strategy. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome affects up to a third of pregnancies when mild cases are counted, arising from fluid retention within a non expandable fibro osseous tunnel and peaking in the third trimester. The distribution spares the little finger because the ulnar nerve does not pass through the tunnel, and nocturnal predominance reflects wrist flexion during sleep. The important clinical division is between sensory symptoms alone, which are managed conservatively, and motor involvement with thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction, which indicates axonal loss and warrants specialist referral. Alternative causes of hand numbness in pregnancy include cervical radiculopathy, which produces neck pain with dermatomal radiation and reflex change, and hypothyroidism or diabetes, which are checked because both predispose to median neuropathy. Most women improve within weeks of delivery, although symptoms that persist beyond three months postpartum, particularly in women who breastfeed, warrant reassessment.
key_points: Sparing of the little finger localises the lesion to the median nerve at the wrist
Nocturnal symptoms reflect wrist flexion during sleep raising tunnel pressure
Neutral position night splinting is first line and is often sufficient
Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction changes the plan to specialist referral
The great majority resolve within weeks to months of delivery
explanation.pearls: Test abductor pollicis brevis specifically by asking her to lift the thumb vertically off the palm against resistance: weakness there, not the severity of the night time tingling, is what converts a splint and reassurance into an urgent referral for decompression.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

subtopic_detail: Painless smooth mobile breast lump in a lactating woman with no fever and no overlying inflammation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman who is four months postpartum and still fully breastfeeding. She found a lump in the outer part of her left breast about three weeks ago and says it has slowly got bigger but does not hurt.

She has had no fever or flu like symptoms, and the lump has not changed with feeding or expressing. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

data_table.Examination: Smooth mobile non tender 3 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, no overlying erythema or warmth, no skin dimpling or nipple change, no axillary lymphadenopathy, right breast normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin and review the breast in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics treat lactational mastitis and its complications, which present with a hot tender wedge of erythema, fever and systemic symptoms. A painless lump with normal overlying skin in an afebrile woman is not infective, so antibiotics would delay assessment by days. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Breast lumps in lactation)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Breast lumps in lactation

options.text: Advise continued feeding from that side and reassess the lump in six weeks
options.rationale: Feeding through a blocked duct is correct management for a lump that appears suddenly, is tender and resolves within a day or two with drainage. A lump present for three weeks that is enlarging and does not change with feeding has already declared itself as something other than a blocked duct. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Arrange a breast ultrasound scan with aspiration of the lesion if indicated
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the first line imaging modality for a breast lump in a woman under thirty five and in lactation, because dense glandular tissue limits mammography and ultrasound reliably separates cystic from solid lesions. A galactocele has a characteristic appearance and aspiration of milky fluid is both diagnostic and therapeutic, while a solid lesion proceeds to core biopsy. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Request bilateral mammography with tomosynthesis at the local imaging centre
options.rationale: Mammography is the primary modality above about thirty five years and remains part of assessment where malignancy is suspected, but lactating breast tissue is markedly dense and reduces its sensitivity substantially. Starting with mammography in a woman of this age risks a falsely reassuring result. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Advise that she wean before any imaging so that the breast can be assessed
options.rationale: Weaning is not required for breast imaging or for core biopsy, both of which are performed safely during lactation, and the small risk of a milk fistula after biopsy does not justify ending breastfeeding. Delaying assessment until involution is complete would postpone diagnosis by months. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Breast lumps in lactation)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Breast lumps in lactation

explanation.summary: A discrete breast lump during lactation must be assessed on its own merits rather than attributed to feeding, because pregnancy associated breast cancer is frequently diagnosed late for exactly that reason. The common benign causes are a blocked duct, which is tender and resolves with drainage within days, an abscess, which is painful with systemic features, and a galactocele, which is a milk retention cyst presenting as a painless enlarging smooth mobile lump. Assessment follows the triple approach of clinical examination, imaging and, where indicated, tissue sampling, with ultrasound as the first imaging test under about thirty five years and in lactation because glandular density limits mammography. A galactocele yields milky fluid on aspiration and usually resolves, whereas any solid or residual lesion requires core biopsy. Neither imaging nor biopsy requires weaning, and lactation should continue through the assessment.
key_points: A persistent lump in lactation is investigated, never attributed to feeding alone
Ultrasound is first line under thirty five years and during lactation
A blocked duct is tender and settles in days; a galactocele is painless and grows
Aspiration of milky fluid is both diagnostic and therapeutic for a galactocele
Imaging and core biopsy are both safe without weaning
explanation.pearls: Apply the same rule in lactation as outside it: any discrete lump still present after two weeks goes to ultrasound, because pregnancy associated breast cancer is typically node positive at diagnosis and the delay is almost always attributable to the lump being ascribed to feeding.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom
Australian Breastfeeding Association: Breast lumps in lactation
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of breast lump

subtopic_detail: Worsening pelvic infection after four days of oral treatment with a complex multiloculated adnexal collection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28 year old woman with five days of lower abdominal pain and an offensive vaginal discharge. Her general practitioner diagnosed pelvic inflammatory disease four days ago and started her on oral doxycycline with metronidazole, which she has taken as directed.

She has got worse rather than better, with rigors overnight and pain now severe enough that she cannot stand up straight. She has vomited twice today and has not been able to keep the tablets down since yesterday evening. She uses a copper intrauterine device and has had a new sexual partner in the past three months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 per minute, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen tender in both iliac fossae with guarding on the right, cervical motion tenderness marked, tender fullness palpable in the right adnexa, purulent discharge at the cervical os
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, white cell count 17.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 184 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), endocervical nucleic acid testing pending, transvaginal ultrasound shows a 6 cm multiloculated thick walled right adnexal collection with internal debris and free pelvic fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the oral antibiotics for a further ten days and review her in clinic
options.rationale: Outpatient oral therapy is appropriate for uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease in a woman who is systemically well and able to take tablets. She has already failed four days of correct oral treatment, is febrile and tachycardic, and is vomiting, all of which are recognised criteria for admission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics with early gynaecological and radiological review
options.rationale: A thick walled multiloculated adnexal collection with sepsis is a tubo ovarian abscess, which requires admission and broad spectrum intravenous therapy covering aerobes, anaerobes and the sexually transmitted organisms. Around three quarters respond to antibiotics alone, and image guided drainage is arranged for collections that fail to improve within 48 to 72 hours, which is why radiology is involved from the outset rather than after failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Add oral fluconazole for candidiasis and repeat the ultrasound in two weeks
options.rationale: Antifungal treatment addresses vulvovaginal candidiasis, which causes itch and a thick white discharge without fever, sepsis or an adnexal mass. Delaying reassessment by two weeks in a septic woman with a 6 cm collection risks rupture and generalised peritonitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopy today for removal of the affected tube and ovary
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for a ruptured abscess, for haemodynamic instability, or for failure of antibiotics with or without drainage, and removing the adnexa is a significant fertility cost in a woman of this age. Most abscesses resolve with antibiotics, so proceeding directly to salpingo oophorectomy is a step too far in a woman who is not peritonitic. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic inflammatory disease)

options.text: Manage as a ruptured ovarian cyst with analgesia and observation on the ward
options.rationale: A ruptured cyst causes sudden severe pain with free fluid and is managed conservatively, and the free fluid here could support that reading. It does not produce a fever of 38.7 degrees Celsius, a C reactive protein of 184 mg/L, purulent cervical discharge or a thick walled loculated mass. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic inflammatory disease)

explanation.summary: Tubo ovarian abscess is a late complication of pelvic inflammatory disease in which infection spreads from the endometrium through the tubes to form a walled off inflammatory mass involving the tube and ovary, and it should be suspected whenever a woman fails to improve on appropriate oral therapy. The infection is polymicrobial, involving anaerobes and enteric organisms as well as the sexually transmitted pathogens that initiated it, so treatment must cover all three groups. Admission criteria for pelvic inflammatory disease in Australian practice include pregnancy, failure of oral therapy, inability to tolerate oral intake, severe illness, a tubo ovarian abscess and diagnostic uncertainty with a surgical differential. Antibiotics alone resolve the majority of abscesses, with image guided aspiration or drainage for larger collections or those not improving over 48 to 72 hours, and surgery is reserved for rupture, instability or treatment failure. Contact tracing, testing for other sexually transmitted infections including human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis, and counselling about the long term risks of tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain form part of the same episode of care.
key_points: Failure to improve on correct oral therapy should prompt imaging for an abscess
The infection is polymicrobial and needs anaerobic and enteric cover as well
Vomiting, sepsis, pregnancy or an abscess are indications for admission
Antibiotics alone resolve most abscesses, with drainage for failure at 48 to 72 hours
Contact tracing and testing for other sexually transmitted infections are part of care
explanation.pearls: Leave the intrauterine device in place while starting antibiotics and reassess at 48 to 72 hours: removing it immediately was long standing practice but does not improve outcomes when effective antibiotics are running, and it removes her contraception at the moment she is least able to discuss alternatives.

subtopic_detail: Severe localised pain over a known fibroid at mid gestation with a mild leucocytosis and a soft uterus between
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy who has had two days of constant severe pain in the right side of her abdomen. She points to one spot above and to the right of her umbilicus and says the pain is worse when anything presses on it.

A fibroid measuring 8 cm was documented on her first trimester scan. She has had no vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid, no urinary symptoms, and no vomiting or change in her bowels. The baby has been moving normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 150 per minute
data_table.Examination: Marked localised tenderness over a firm mass in the right upper uterus, uterus soft and non tender elsewhere with no tightenings palpable, no renal angle tenderness, no rebound or guarding in the right iliac fossa, cervix long and closed on speculum with no discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (6.0-16.0 in pregnancy), C reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine shows no growth, ultrasound shows an 8 cm fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture and central cystic change, normal liquor volume, normal foetal growth, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Take her to theatre for laparotomy and myomectomy of the painful fibroid
options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries a substantial risk of uncontrollable haemorrhage from the hypervascular gravid uterus and of pregnancy loss, and is confined to rare situations such as a torted pedunculated fibroid that cannot be managed otherwise. A fibroid within the uterine wall with pain alone does not meet that threshold. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange urgent surgical review for appendicectomy through a right sided incision
options.rationale: Appendicitis is the commonest non obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy and the appendix is displaced upward at this gestation, making it a genuine consideration. The pain here is exactly localised to an imaged fibroid with cystic change and there is no rebound, guarding or gastrointestinal upset. (Source: RANZCOG: Abdominal pain in pregnancy)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics for presumed intrauterine infection
options.rationale: Chorioamnionitis produces maternal tachycardia with a tender uterus throughout, foetal tachycardia, offensive discharge and usually ruptured membranes. The uterus here is soft and non tender away from the fibroid, the membranes are intact and the cardiotocograph is normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence nifedipine tocolysis and give intramuscular betamethasone
options.rationale: Tocolysis and antenatal corticosteroids are the response to established preterm labour, which requires regular painful contractions with cervical change. She has a long closed cervix, no palpable tightenings and constant rather than intermittent pain. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Admit for analgesia including a short course of a non steroidal anti inflammatory
options.rationale: Constant exquisitely localised pain over a rapidly growing fibroid with a low grade fever, a mild leucocytosis and heterogeneous echotexture with central cystic change is red degeneration, which occurs when the fibroid outgrows its blood supply and infarcts. It is managed conservatively with analgesia, and a short course of a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug is effective and acceptable before 32 weeks, after which ductal constriction and oligohydramnios become the limiting concerns. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Fibroids enlarge under the influence of pregnancy hormones and increased uterine blood flow, and around one in ten become symptomatic, most often in the second trimester. Red or carneous degeneration occurs when growth outstrips perfusion and the fibroid infarcts, producing constant severe pain localised precisely over the lesion, a low grade fever, a mild leucocytosis and a modest rise in inflammatory markers. This inflammatory picture is the trap, since it mimics appendicitis, pyelonephritis and chorioamnionitis, and the discriminators are the exact localisation of tenderness to an imaged fibroid and a uterus that is soft and non tender elsewhere. Management is conservative with hydration and analgesia, and symptoms settle over days to a week. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are used for short courses before 32 weeks, since after that gestation they risk premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios, and surgery during pregnancy is avoided because the gravid uterus bleeds heavily.
key_points: Red degeneration produces constant pain localised exactly over the fibroid
Low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and raised inflammatory markers are expected
A soft non tender uterus away from the fibroid argues against intrauterine infection
Management is conservative with hydration and analgesia over several days
Short course non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are acceptable before 32 weeks
explanation.pearls: Limit the non steroidal course to about 48 hours and stop it entirely from 32 weeks: beyond that gestation indomethacin and its relatives constrict the ductus arteriosus and reduce foetal urine output, so paracetamol and opioid analgesia become the only options for a fibroid that degenerates late in pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Fluctuant swelling at the posterior introitus in a woman past forty presenting for drainage
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 52 year old woman with four days of increasing pain and swelling on the left side of the vaginal opening, now bad enough that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably.

She went through menopause at 50 and has had no previous vulval problems, no vulval itch and no postmenopausal bleeding. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medication and has never smoked.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender fluctuant 5 cm swelling at the posterior aspect of the left labium majus displacing the introitus medially, overlying skin erythematous and intact with no induration of surrounding tissue, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no white atrophic vulval skin
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C reactive protein pending, urine dipstick negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Drain the cavity and send a biopsy of the gland wall for histology
options.rationale: Drainage relieves the acute problem, and a wall biopsy is taken because carcinoma of the Bartholin gland, though rare, presents as an apparent abscess or cyst and is the reason a first presentation over the age of forty is treated differently from one in a younger woman. Taking the specimen at the time of drainage avoids a second procedure and detects a tumour that simple drainage would leave undiagnosed. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Perform simple incision and drainage with a scalpel and pack the cavity
options.rationale: Simple incision and drainage relieves pain quickly but the tract closes within days and recurrence follows in roughly one in three women, which is why a catheter or marsupialisation is preferred for durable epithelialisation. It also produces no tissue for histology in a woman of an age where that matters. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Insert a balloon tipped catheter into the cavity and leave it for four weeks
options.rationale: A balloon tipped catheter is an excellent office procedure that allows a drainage tract to epithelialise and markedly reduces recurrence compared with incision alone, and it would be the preferred answer in a younger woman. On its own it still does not provide the histological sample that a first presentation after forty requires. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Treat with oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and warm baths for five days
options.rationale: Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis or immunosuppression, and they do not resolve a fluctuant collection, which requires drainage to relieve the pressure. Managing a 5 cm fluctuant abscess medically leaves her in pain and unable to walk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange elective excision of the whole gland once the inflammation has settled
options.rationale: Gland excision is definitive but is associated with significant bleeding from the vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia, so it is reserved for repeated recurrence after lesser procedures or for proven malignancy. It is not the first intervention for an initial presentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses arise when the duct at the posterior introitus obstructs, and abscesses are usually polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora rather than caused by a single sexually transmitted organism, although gonorrhoea and chlamydia are tested for when risk factors exist. The management principle is to create a drainage tract that stays open long enough to epithelialise, which is achieved with a balloon tipped catheter left in place for several weeks or with marsupialisation, since simple incision and drainage recurs in around a third of women. Antibiotics are an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features or immunosuppression rather than a substitute for drainage. The age related rule matters clinically: primary carcinoma of the Bartholin gland accounts for a small percentage of vulval malignancy and typically presents in the sixth decade as a persistent cyst or abscess, so a first presentation over about forty years warrants biopsy of the gland wall at the time of drainage. Features such as a hard fixed mass, ulceration or inguinal lymphadenopathy require excisional biopsy rather than drainage.
key_points: The aim is a drainage tract that stays open, not simply evacuation of pus
Simple incision and drainage recurs in around one in three women
Antibiotics are adjunctive and do not replace drainage of a fluctuant collection
A first presentation after about forty years warrants biopsy of the gland wall
A hard fixed or ulcerated mass requires excisional biopsy rather than drainage
explanation.pearls: Take the wall biopsy at the moment of drainage in any woman over forty presenting with a first Bartholin swelling: adenoid cystic and squamous carcinomas of the gland characteristically masquerade as a recurrent cyst for months, and the only opportunity to catch them early is the tissue taken when the cavity is opened.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

subtopic_detail: Absent periods with cyclical pain after repeated uterine instrumentation and no withdrawal bleed on progestogen
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman who has not had a period for eight months. Her last pregnancy ended in a vaginal birth complicated by heavy bleeding, and she had two operations to remove retained tissue from the womb in the following fortnight.

She stopped breastfeeding four months ago and describes cramping lower abdominal pain for two or three days each month with no bleeding at all. She is not using contraception and would like another pregnancy. She has had no hot flushes, no galactorrhoea and no change in weight, appetite or energy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, no acne or hirsutism, breasts with no expressible discharge, uterus anteverted normal size and non tender, no adnexal masses, visual fields normal to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 5.8 IU/L, oestradiol 340 pmol/L, prolactin and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, no withdrawal bleeding after a ten day course of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the progestogen challenge at a higher dose over fourteen days
options.rationale: Repeating the challenge is reasonable when the first course was too short or adherence was uncertain, since a false negative result then misclassifies the patient. Here the failure to bleed despite an oestradiol of 340 pmol/L already shows the endometrium cannot respond, which is a structural answer rather than a dosing problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Secondary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure the anti Mullerian hormone concentration to assess ovarian reserve
options.rationale: Anti Mullerian hormone quantifies the remaining follicle pool and guides fertility treatment planning, but it does not explain amenorrhoea and would not alter management here. Normal gonadotrophins with an oestradiol in the follicular range already demonstrate that the ovaries are functioning. (Source: RANZCOG: Secondary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive to re establish a regular bleeding pattern
options.rationale: Cyclical hormones restore withdrawal bleeding when the endometrium is intact but under stimulated, as in hypothalamic amenorrhoea. Prescribing them to a woman seeking pregnancy who cannot bleed because the cavity is obliterated delays diagnosis and provides contraception she does not want. (Source: RANZCOG: Secondary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy to assess the cavity and divide any adhesions found
options.rationale: Normal gonadotrophins with an oestradiol confirming ovarian activity, no withdrawal bleed and cyclical pain after repeated instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus localise the problem to the endometrial cavity rather than the axis. Hysteroscopy both confirms intrauterine adhesions and treats them under direct vision, which is the only way to restore the cavity and her fertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Secondary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound scan to measure the endometrial thickness
options.rationale: Ultrasound may show a thin or irregular endometrium with bright interfaces and is a reasonable screening test, but it is insensitive for adhesions and a normal appearance does not exclude them. It also offers no treatment, so a woman with this history requires hysteroscopy regardless of the scan result. (Source: RANZCOG: Secondary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is worked through by excluding pregnancy, then measuring prolactin, thyroid stimulating hormone and gonadotrophins to separate hypothalamic, pituitary, ovarian and outflow tract causes. Normal gonadotrophins with an oestradiol in the follicular range indicate a functioning axis and ovaries, so a failure to bleed after progestogen points to the endometrium or the outflow tract. Intrauterine adhesions are the classic cause in a woman who has had curettage of a recently pregnant uterus, particularly when performed more than once or in the presence of infection, because the postpartum endometrium is thin and the basal layer is easily damaged. Cyclical pain without bleeding indicates functioning endometrium trapped above obstruction. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis under direct vision is both diagnostic and therapeutic, and recurrence is common, so postoperative strategies include oestrogen therapy and physical barriers with planned second look hysteroscopy.
key_points: Normal gonadotrophins with a follicular oestradiol exclude ovarian and axis causes
No withdrawal bleed despite adequate oestrogen localises the problem to the endometrium
Repeated curettage of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent
Cyclical pain without bleeding indicates functioning endometrium above obstruction
Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is diagnostic and therapeutic, with recurrence common
explanation.pearls: Interpret the progestogen challenge in the light of the oestradiol rather than on its own: a woman with an oestradiol above 200 pmol/L who does not bleed has an endometrium that cannot respond, and that single pairing of results moves the investigation from the hypothalamus to the uterine cavity.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea investigation

subtopic_detail: Birth planning after a previous repaired third degree perineal tear with normal continence and normal anorectal testing
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a woman at 34 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first baby weighed 3.6 kg and was born with a vacuum after a long second stage, and she sustained a tear involving the anal sphincter that was repaired in theatre.

She has no leakage of wind or stool, no faecal urgency and no soiling, and says her bowel control is the same as it was before her first pregnancy. Estimated foetal weight on a growth scan last week was on the 55th centile. She has read online that she must have a caesarean and wants to know what you advise.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142 per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysiofundal height 34 cm, cephalic presentation, perineum with a healed midline scar and no defect palpable on digital assessment, resting and squeeze anal tone subjectively normal
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound shows an intact external and internal anal sphincter, anorectal manometry resting and squeeze pressures within normal limits, St Mark's incontinence score zero

lead_in: What would you first recommend regarding her mode of birth?

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to protect the sphincter
options.rationale: Elective caesarean is recommended when a woman has persistent symptoms or abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, because further vaginal birth then risks decompensating a sphincter with reduced reserve. Neither applies here, and recommending it universally exposes women to the risks of abdominal delivery for no measurable benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)

options.text: Recommend a planned vaginal birth and discuss the small risk of recurrent injury
options.rationale: A woman who is asymptomatic with an intact sphincter on endoanal ultrasound and normal manometry has sphincter reserve comparable to a woman who has never sustained an injury, and can be advised that vaginal birth is appropriate. The recurrence risk of a further sphincter injury is in the order of five to seven per cent, and that figure forms the basis of the discussion rather than a reason to change route. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)

options.text: Recommend a vaginal birth with a routine mediolateral episiotomy at delivery
options.rationale: Routine episiotomy in a woman with a previous sphincter injury has not been shown to prevent recurrence and introduces its own morbidity, so it is performed for a clinical indication at the time rather than by policy. The measures that do help are a controlled slow delivery of the head and manual perineal protection. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)

options.text: Offer either route without a recommendation and leave the decision entirely to her
options.rationale: Her values and preferences must shape the final decision, but she has asked for advice and the testing has produced a clear clinical discriminator, so declining to give a recommendation withholds the information she came for. Shared decision making means offering a defensible recommendation and then exploring her view of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)

options.text: Refer to a colorectal surgeon for secondary sphincter repair before she gives birth
options.rationale: Secondary sphincter repair is considered for women with a persisting sphincter defect and significant incontinence that has failed conservative treatment, and is usually deferred until childbearing is complete. Operating on a sphincter shown to be intact and functioning normally offers nothing to gain. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury complicates roughly three per cent of vaginal births in Australia and around six per cent of first vaginal births, with instrumental delivery, a large baby, a long second stage and shoulder dystocia among the recognised risk factors. Counselling for a subsequent birth is driven by two things: current symptoms and objective sphincter assessment with endoanal ultrasound and anorectal manometry. A woman who is asymptomatic with normal investigations has the same expected outcome from vaginal birth as a woman without a previous injury, and the risk of recurrence sits at roughly five to seven per cent. A woman with symptoms or with a demonstrable sphincter defect or low squeeze pressures should be advised that a further vaginal birth risks decompensation into frank incontinence, and elective caesarean is recommended. All women with a previous injury deserve a documented antenatal discussion, and intrapartum care focuses on a controlled delivery of the head, manual perineal protection and prompt recognition and repair of any new injury by an appropriately trained clinician.
key_points: Symptoms plus endoanal ultrasound and manometry drive the counselling
Asymptomatic women with normal testing can be advised to have a vaginal birth
Recurrence risk of a further sphincter injury is about five to seven per cent
Symptoms or a sphincter defect shift the recommendation to elective caesarean
Routine episiotomy does not prevent recurrent sphincter injury
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about urgency and flatal incontinence rather than about soiling alone: loss of control of wind or an inability to defer defaecation for more than a few minutes is the earliest marker of reduced sphincter reserve, and its presence changes the recommendation to elective caesarean even when endoanal imaging looks intact.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Perineal management
BMJ Best Practice: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: Entry pain limited to the vestibule reproduced by cotton bud testing with normal skin and negative swabs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old woman who has had eighteen months of burning pain at the entrance to the vagina that occurs only with penetration and with tampon insertion. She has no pain walking, sitting or cycling, and none at any other time.

She has completed three courses of antifungal treatment prescribed over the past year without benefit, and has had no discharge, itch or odour throughout. She is in a supportive relationship, has no history of sexual assault, and finds the situation increasingly distressing.

data_table.Examination: Vulval skin normal in colour and texture with no erythema, fissuring, whitening or architectural change, cotton bud testing reproduces sharp pain at the posterior vestibule at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions and is painless on the labia majora and perineum, pelvic floor tone normal on digital examination with no guarding and no involuntary contraction on approach
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal and endocervical swabs negative for Candida species, bacterial vaginosis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a longer course of oral fluconazole for resistant vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.rationale: Extended azole therapy is used for recurrent candidiasis confirmed on culture, including non albicans species that need alternative agents. Three failed courses with repeatedly negative swabs and no discharge or itch make this diagnosis untenable, and repeated empirical treatment is itself a cause of vulval irritation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply a topical oestrogen cream to the vestibule nightly for eight weeks
options.rationale: Vestibular oestrogen helps when the tissue is atrophic, which occurs after menopause or with hypo oestrogenic states including some combined contraceptive users, and the skin then looks pale and thin with loss of elasticity. Her vulval skin is normal in colour and texture, so there is no atrophy to reverse. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval pain)

options.text: Refer to a gynaecologist for surgical excision of the painful vestibular tissue
options.rationale: Vestibulectomy has reasonable success rates in carefully selected women, but it is a last resort after multimodal conservative treatment has failed over a sustained period, and it is irreversible. Offering surgery before any physical or psychological therapy has been tried inverts the treatment ladder. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval pain)

options.text: Commence a low dose tricyclic antidepressant taken at night for neuropathic pain
options.rationale: Low dose amitriptyline is used for generalised unprovoked vulvodynia, where pain is constant and spontaneous rather than triggered by contact, and it has a limited role in localised provoked pain. It is an adjunct rather than a starting point, and its anticholinergic effects are poorly tolerated in young women. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval pain)

options.text: Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy alongside education and psychosexual support
options.rationale: Pain confined to the vestibule and reproduced by light touch on cotton bud testing, with normal skin and negative swabs, is provoked vestibulodynia, and the treatment with the strongest evidence is pelvic floor physiotherapy combined with education about the condition and psychological or psychosexual therapy. Multimodal treatment addresses the peripheral sensitisation, the secondary muscle changes and the distress and avoidance that maintain the cycle. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval pain)

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of at least three months duration without an identifiable cause, and is classified by whether the pain is localised or generalised and whether it is provoked or spontaneous. Provoked vestibulodynia is the commonest form in premenopausal women, presents with entry dyspareunia and pain on tampon insertion, and is diagnosed by the cotton bud test reproducing sharp pain confined to the vestibule with a normal looking vulva. The diagnosis is regularly delayed for years while women receive repeated antifungal courses, and that delay itself contributes to distress, avoidance and relationship strain. It must be distinguished from dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, which alter the skin, from infection, and from vaginismus, where involuntary pelvic floor contraction prevents entry. Management is multimodal and evidence supports pelvic floor physiotherapy, cognitive behavioural and psychosexual therapy and topical local anaesthetic before intercourse, with tricyclics, gabapentinoids and vestibulectomy reserved for refractory disease.
key_points: Cotton bud testing localises the pain and is the key examination manoeuvre
The vulva looks entirely normal, which is what separates it from a dermatosis
Repeated empirical antifungal treatment is the usual pattern of delayed diagnosis
Normal pelvic floor tone on approach distinguishes it from vaginismus
Physiotherapy with psychosexual therapy has the strongest evidence base
explanation.pearls: Map the pain with a cotton bud at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions of the vestibule before touching anything else: sharp pain there with painless labia majora confirms localised provoked vestibulodynia in one minute and spares the woman another year of antifungal prescriptions.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Vulval pain clinic guidance

subtopic_detail: Adnexal gestational sac alongside a live intrauterine pregnancy after embryo transfer with free pelvic fluid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a 32 year old woman at 7 weeks by dates who conceived through in vitro fertilisation with the transfer of two embryos. She has four hours of right sided lower abdominal pain and has passed a small amount of dark blood vaginally.

She describes the pain as constant and increasing, with a new ache at the tip of her right shoulder. She has vomited twice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and uncomfortable, abdomen tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding, cervical os closed with a small amount of dark blood in the vault
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 48000 IU/L, haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a foetal pole and cardiac activity at 7 weeks, a separate right adnexal sac containing a yolk sac and a foetal pole, and echogenic free fluid extending to the hepatorenal recess

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopy with removal of the affected fallopian tube
options.rationale: A viable intrauterine pregnancy coexisting with an adnexal pregnancy makes this heterotopic, and with tachycardia, hypotension and echogenic fluid reaching the hepatorenal recess the tubal pregnancy has ruptured, so surgery is required regardless of the intrauterine sac. Salpingectomy is chosen over tube conserving surgery because persistent trophoblast after salpingostomy occurs in up to one in five women and is normally treated with methotrexate, which cannot be given while a wanted intrauterine pregnancy continues. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate calculated by body surface area
options.rationale: Methotrexate is the medical option for an unruptured tubal pregnancy meeting size, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin and stability criteria, none of which is met here. It is also an antifolate teratogen that would destroy the intrauterine pregnancy, making it absolutely contraindicated whenever a wanted intrauterine gestation coexists. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopy with opening of the tube and removal of the trophoblast
options.rationale: Salpingostomy preserves the tube and is preferred when the contralateral tube is absent or damaged and future fertility depends on it. Its drawback is persistent trophoblast, which is detected by serial beta human chorionic gonadotrophin and rescued with methotrexate, and neither surveillance nor rescue is possible while an intrauterine pregnancy is producing the hormone and precluding the drug. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Admit for observation with serial beta human chorionic gonadotrophin measurement
options.rationale: Serial hormone measurement is the backbone of expectant management for a pregnancy of unknown location or a small declining ectopic in a stable woman. It is uninterpretable in a heterotopic pregnancy because the intrauterine sac drives the level, and it is unsafe in a woman who is already tachycardic and hypotensive with free fluid. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in forty eight hours with the fertility unit
options.rationale: A repeat scan resolves diagnostic uncertainty when the initial images are equivocal and the woman is stable and pain free. The scan here is already diagnostic, showing two separate gestations and haemoperitoneum, and a further two days would be spent bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy is the simultaneous presence of an intrauterine and an extrauterine gestation, occurring in roughly one in thirty thousand spontaneous conceptions but in the order of one in one hundred after assisted reproduction, where multiple embryo transfer and tubal disease both raise the risk. The diagnostic trap is that identifying an intrauterine pregnancy normally excludes an ectopic, so clinicians stop looking, and the beta human chorionic gonadotrophin is useless because the intrauterine sac drives the level regardless of what the adnexa are doing. Any woman who has conceived through assisted reproduction and presents with pain or free fluid therefore needs deliberate examination of both adnexa even when an intrauterine sac is seen. Management of the ectopic component is surgical, since methotrexate would terminate the wanted intrauterine pregnancy, and salpingectomy is generally preferred over salpingostomy because the usual rescue for persistent trophoblast is unavailable. With prompt surgery the intrauterine pregnancy continues to term in the majority of cases, and anti D immunoglobulin is given to women who are rhesus D negative.
key_points: Assisted reproduction raises heterotopic risk to roughly one in one hundred
Seeing an intrauterine sac does not exclude a coexisting ectopic pregnancy
Beta human chorionic gonadotrophin cannot be interpreted when both exist
Methotrexate is contraindicated because it would terminate the wanted pregnancy
Salpingectomy is preferred since persistent trophoblast cannot be rescued medically
explanation.pearls: Ask the sonographer to sweep both adnexa in every woman with pain after embryo transfer even once a live intrauterine pregnancy is seen: the presence of an intrauterine sac is the single commonest reason a heterotopic pregnancy is missed until it ruptures, and free fluid in the hepatorenal recess means the woman is already bleeding into her abdomen.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Early pregnancy assessment
